title: Synthetic chemomechanical engines whose efficiency approaches biological molecular motors

concept.text: The innovation would be an autonomous synthetic molecular assembly or material that repeatedly converts chemical fuel into useful mechanical work with high efficiency. A defined chemical reaction would drive a designed molecular cycle, producing rotation, displacement or contraction against a load. The motor components would be synthetic rather than evolved proteins. The target combines sustained operation, measurable work output and efficient use of chemical free energy; the supplied evidence does not establish that this combination has been achieved.

Chemomechanical coupling describes how fuel-consuming reactions are linked to mechanical steps. Tight stoichiometric coupling means that fuel consumption reliably accompanies productive motion, with few unproductive reaction cycles. High efficiency additionally requires the useful work delivered to capture a substantial fraction of the chemical free energy consumed. Reliable directionality or a fixed number of fuel molecules per motor turn does not, by itself, establish high efficiency. A convincing engine must therefore connect measurements of motion and load to measurements of fuel consumption under the same operating conditions.

significance.text: Efficient, durable and designable chemical-to-mechanical conversion would substantially expand the capabilities of synthetic molecular actuators. Chemical reactions could power useful motion directly, without an intervening heat engine. The documented artificial motor already establishes a mechanism for accumulating force and elastic energy in a polymer gel, so the prospective advance is sustained work under load with substantially improved energy use, rather than the first demonstration of chemically powered actuation.

Biological motors provide motivation, but comparisons require matching the input and output being measured. ATP synthase uses a proton electrochemical gradient to produce ATP, whereas the proposed engine is assessed by mechanical work delivered per chemical free energy consumed. Muscle contraction is a closer functional analogy to mechanical actuation. Neither analogy supplies a general design method for synthetic engines, and a percentage measured for ATP synthesis cannot automatically serve as a mechanical-work efficiency benchmark.

Conditional synthesis: a successful engine could support chemically powered soft actuators, materials that perform repeated mechanical tasks, and eventually medical or manufacturing devices. Those applications would require additional evidence of useful power, durability, controllability, integration and manufacturability. Success with one reaction cycle and polymer architecture would establish a particular technology; compatibility with arbitrary fuels, materials or operating environments would remain a separate engineering ambition.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is sustained net mechanical work against a measured load, with quantified work per consumed fuel molecule and efficient coupling throughout repeated operation. The supplied sources establish artificial rotary motors, information-ratchet analysis and catalysis-driven gel contraction, but do not demonstrate the proposed combination of efficiency and endurance. Because the supplied freshness record contains no search evidence, this is a target defined by the record, not a verified claim that no system anywhere had achieved it by 1 November 2026.

A concrete barrier is preventing fuel consumption from continuing without useful mechanical output. In the documented gel, motor-catalysed carbodiimide hydration continued after contraction stopped, provided fuel remained or was replenished. This establishes an unproductive operating regime in that system, without determining its numerical efficiency. Improved engines must coordinate reaction kinetics, directional motion and mechanical loading so that the chemical cycle remains productive as resistance and stored elastic energy increase. The paper identifies both the fuel-to-waste chemical-potential difference and kinetic asymmetry of the engine cycle as relevant to energy transduction.

Engineering synthesis: repeated useful operation also requires a way to reset or complete the mechanical cycle while retaining positive net work, maintain fuel delivery and waste removal, and avoid progressive loss of motor or material function. A finite contraction can accumulate elastic energy without providing a reusable work cycle. Scaling from molecular motion to material output therefore requires coordinated mechanics as well as chemical design, while performance must be assessed under load rather than inferred from visible movement alone.

Measurement is part of the breakthrough. Work delivered to an external load, energy stored elastically, reaction heat and chemical free energy consumed are different quantities. The engine must be characterised well enough to distinguish them and to include background fuel consumption and auxiliary chemical inputs. Without that accounting, contraction or an estimate of stored energy cannot establish efficient conversion of fuel into useful output.

current_state.text: Amano and coauthors, Nature Chemistry 14, 530–537 (2022), DOI 10.1038/s41557-022-00899-z, analysed a minimalist autonomous chemically driven synthetic molecular motor using information thermodynamics. The supplied PubMed abstract describes chemical-to-mechanical free-energy transfer and how power strokes can affect velocity, transfer efficiency and fuel molecules consumed per cycle. Access in the supplied review was limited to the abstract, which does not state an efficiency of 10⁻⁸. It therefore supports the mechanism and measurement priorities, but does not verify that numerical value or the full paper’s quantitative conclusions.

Peng-Lai Wang, Stephen Borsley, Alexander Power, Rosangela Cavasso, Nicolas Giuseppone and David A. Leigh reported artificial catalysis-driven rotary motors embedded in a polymer gel in Nature 637, 594–600, published online on 15 January 2025, DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-08288-x. The motors powered contraction to approximately 70% of the gel’s original volume, meaning an approximately 30% volume decrease. The volume change was inferred from the decrease in projected surface area under an assumption of isotropic contraction. The supplied review had full article HTML and PDF text, including the complete author list; its assessment relied on prose and captions, without inspection of figure images.

Supplementary section S8.2 of the same study tentatively estimated elastic energy storage of 0.000204 J, equivalent to 0.116 kJ per mole of motor. That denominator is motor quantity, not consumed fuel, and the estimate is not a measured chemical-free-energy conversion efficiency. Some supplementary equations were garbled in extraction, and the underlying plots were not inspected in the supplied review, preventing independent validation of the model calculation. The estimate remains relevant evidence of attempted energy accounting, with those limitations preserved.

The 2025 gel result establishes macroscopic chemical-to-mechanical actuation and estimated stored elastic energy. It does not establish efficient sustained cycling or continuous useful work delivery. Continued fuel consumption after contraction stalled is a documented limitation of this implementation. Neither that limitation nor the absence of a reported efficiency proves the result false; they bound what the demonstration supports.

The earlier research attributed two efficiency figures to Leighton and Sivak, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry 76, 379–403 (2025), DOI 10.1146/annurev-physchem-082423-030023: 70–90% for ATP synthase, attributed there to Silverstein (2014), and an order of 10⁻⁸ for de novo synthetic free-energy transduction, attributed to Amano and coauthors. The source index lists an ar5iv preprint URL for that review, but no retained document was supplied. These remain unverified reported attributions in this record. Silverstein’s source was not opened, and Amano’s available abstract does not supply the latter number. Neither figure should be treated here as a validated benchmark, especially a field-wide benchmark for synthetic motors.

Evidence boundary: the dated achievements above describe the supplied evidence, not a comprehensive account of the field as of 1 November 2026. No bounded freshness search was provided, so later progress and the present-day openness of the target remain unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: demonstrate an autonomous synthetic molecular assembly or material, powered by a defined chemical reaction, delivering positive cumulative net mechanical work against a measured load for at least 1,000 explicitly defined operating cycles. Define whether a cycle means a molecular revolution, a complete material contraction-and-reset sequence, or another reproducible operation, and explain how molecular cycles relate to useful material output. Account for any reset or replenishment procedure. The 1,000-cycle threshold is a proposed endurance target, not a published consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Autonomous synthetic engine sustains positive net work across 1,000 cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: measure load and displacement to determine mechanical work, and measure directional bias and fuel-to-product conversion on the same operating sample. Determine chemical free energy consumed from reaction thermodynamics and measured reactant and product activities under operating conditions. Use independent calorimetry to check the energy balance; heat measurement alone does not determine the Gibbs free-energy input. Include background fuel consumption, auxiliary chemical inputs and changes in stored energy, so that preloaded elastic energy or one-time material changes are not mistaken for sustained fuel-powered output.
completion_criteria.label: Same-sample mechanical work and chemical free-energy accounting with calorimetric validation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed efficiency milestone: require cumulative net mechanical work delivered to exceed 20% of the total chemical free energy consumed over the stated run, with reported uncertainty. Report efficiency alongside work rate, load, cycle rate and changes in performance during operation. This would demonstrate a substantial conversion capability under specified conditions, but 20% alone would establish neither near-unit efficiency nor parity with biological motors. Any biological comparison should use an explicitly matched input-output definition.
completion_criteria.label: Cumulative net work exceeds 20% of chemical free energy consumed

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: reproduce the result across independently prepared samples and, preferably, in an independent laboratory. Use controls that distinguish the designed motor cycle from background catalysis and passive material changes. State the demonstrated fuel, waste concentrations, solvent, temperature, load range, material architecture, lifetime and regeneration requirements. Finite tests establish demonstrated breadth and repeatability within those boundaries; they cannot establish universal compatibility with fuels or materials.
completion_criteria.label: Independent samples reproduce results with controls and stated operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: THR-02, Useful heat engines that are simultaneously efficient, powerful, and steady, shares the challenge of combining conversion efficiency with useful output rate and sustained operation. THR-07 instead takes chemical free energy as its input and mechanical work as its output, without requiring an intervening heat engine. THR-04, Bulk electronic heat–charge decoupling sufficient for engine-class solid-state conversion, and THR-06, A single-absorber solar converter that uses non-thermal carriers to pass the detailed-balance limit, also concern improved energy conversion, but use electronic transport or photogenerated carriers rather than a chemically driven motor cycle.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-12, Predictive thermodynamic design of far-from-equilibrium chemical reaction networks, is closely related through reaction kinetics, chemical driving and dissipation. Such a theory could help design motor cycles, while THR-07 requires a physical demonstration of mechanical output and efficiency. THR-09, A thermodynamic design theory of self-replicators, confirmed by a predicted non-biological replicator, likewise concerns chemically maintained organisation, but its defining output is replication rather than work delivered to a load.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-01, A computable thermodynamic potential for far-from-equilibrium continuum transport, and THR-11, Operational temperature and entropy for far-from-equilibrium matter, concern general descriptions and measurements of nonequilibrium systems. They could inform analysis of fuel transport, dissipation or operating states in a chemomechanical material. THR-07 remains an actuator capability that could be demonstrated within a particular system without first resolving either general theoretical programme.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-03, General-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale, and THR-08, Equilibrium sampling computers operating near thermal energy per sample, overlap through information thermodynamics and energy accounting. The information-ratchet description of a synthetic motor does not make it a general-purpose computer or an equilibrium sampler. THR-05, A size-extensive quantum advantage in thermodynamic performance, would require a distinct demonstration of quantum advantage; THR-07 does not require such an advantage. THR-10, A laboratory measurement of the Unruh temperature, has only broad thermodynamic overlap and a separate experimental objective.

unresolved_issues: Whether sustained high-efficiency synthetic chemomechanical work had been demonstrated elsewhere by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no freshness search record was supplied.
The exact wording, definitions, scope and reference attributions behind the Leighton–Sivak efficiency figures remain unverified; the missing source is not evidence that the figures are false.
Amano’s full quantitative results cannot be established from the supplied PubMed abstract alone.
The supplementary stored-energy calculation cannot be independently validated from the supplied review because some equations were garbled and underlying plots were not inspected.
The 2025 gel’s mechanical-work efficiency relative to chemical free energy consumed, and its ability to support repeated net-work cycles, are not established by the supplied evidence.
The proposed cycle definition, operating load, uncertainty tolerance and matched biological comparison would need to be specified for a particular experimental implementation.

brief.title: Efficient tiny engines powered by chemical fuel
possible: Soft materials could repeatedly pull, turn or contract using chemical fuel directly. Tiny synthetic motors would drive the motion on their own, delivering useful work against resistance while capturing a substantial share of the energy their fuel releases.
why: This would give designers a way to power repeated mechanical tasks in soft materials directly through chemistry. Efficient, durable motors could eventually support medical or manufacturing devices.

sources.showed: This review discusses energy-conversion efficiency in biological and synthetic molecular systems.
sources.cited_for: It provides context for comparing biological and synthetic energy conversion.
sources.not_established: Its reported efficiency figures do not establish a matched benchmark for useful mechanical work.

sources.showed: Their theoretical analysis explained how chemical energy drives a synthetic molecular motor. It found that changes in molecular shape can affect speed, energy transfer and fuel use without setting the direction of motion.
sources.quote: In line with kinetic analysis, we find that power strokes do not affect the directionality of chemically driven machines.
sources.cited_for: Directional motion alone does not establish efficient conversion of fuel into work.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not demonstrate a durable synthetic engine delivering efficient, repeated work against a load.

sources.showed: Synthetic rotary motors twisted linked molecular chains in a gel, shrinking its estimated volume by about 30%. Changing the fuelling system reversed rotation, allowing expansion and renewed contraction.
sources.quote: Continued powered twisting of the strands in the new direction causes the gel to re-contract.
sources.cited_for: Artificial motors can turn chemical fuel into force and visible material movement.
sources.not_established: The gel kept consuming fuel after contraction stopped; efficient sustained work over repeated cycles was not demonstrated.

shown: Wang and collaborators made a gel contract using chemically powered synthetic motors. Reversing their rotation made it expand and contract again. This connects molecular motion to material movement, but fuel consumption continued after contraction stalled.
missing: An engine must deliver repeated net work against a measured load, including the energy cost of resetting it.
Measurements must connect useful work to chemical energy consumed, including wasted fuel and other chemical inputs.
Repeated operation must preserve motor and material function while supplying fuel and removing waste.

milestones.label: An autonomous engine delivers useful work across 1,000 cycles
milestones.explanation: A chemically powered synthetic engine would have to deliver positive cumulative net work across 1,000 clearly defined cycles, accounting for resets. This would establish endurance beyond a finite contraction.

milestones.label: Work and fuel measurements close the energy balance
milestones.explanation: The same sample would need measurements of work, direction, fuel conversion and available chemical energy, with independent heat measurements checking the balance. This would distinguish fuel-powered work from stored energy.

milestones.label: Useful work exceeds 20% of chemical energy consumed
milestones.explanation: Cumulative net work would have to exceed 20% of consumed chemical energy, with uncertainty and operating performance reported. This would establish substantial conversion under defined conditions.

milestones.label: Independent samples reproduce the result within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Independently prepared samples would have to reproduce performance with controls and stated operating limits, preferably in another laboratory. This would establish repeatability and distinguish motor action from passive changes.

uncertain: A molecular turn and a complete material contraction-and-reset cycle are different; their relationship to useful output needs a clear definition.
The proposed endurance and efficiency thresholds are targets, rather than agreed standards for matching biological motors.
Comparisons with biological motors require matching the energy input and useful output being measured.

page.title: Synthetic chemomechanical motors
page.definition: An autonomous motor built from synthetic, nonprotein components repeatedly converts chemical fuel into net work against a load. Its thermodynamic efficiency—the external mechanical work divided by chemical free energy consumed—matches that of isolated F1-ATPase, an ATP-driven rotary enzyme, using the comparison defined below.

goal.need: Chemical fuel can sustain directional molecular motion while transferring little free energy into mechanical dynamics. Amano and coauthors quantified this loss in an experimentally parameterized model at 10 mmol l−1 motor and 30 mmol l−1 fuel. The goal is greater external mechanical work per unit chemical free energy consumed.

figures.caption: Performance estimates for the synthetic rotary motor model analysed by Amano and coauthors.
rows: Fuel molecules consumed per motor cycle
figures.note: The efficiency describes chemical free energy transferred into mechanical dynamics; it is not a measured external-load work efficiency.

statements.quote: Through these collaborations, we aim to construct a molecular system autonomously and efficiently converting various energies.
statements.context: Research area 8006 includes artificial, biological and hybrid molecular systems.

statements.quote: the energy content of the fuel-to-waste reaction should be closely matched to the energy requirement of the task.

completion.title: A synthetic motor matches F1-ATPase's maximum external-load efficiency at positive power.
completion.criterion: A synthetic nonprotein motor operates autonomously at steady state with positive net external mechanical power and η_syn≥η_F1,max. Here η=P_load/P_chem; η_F1,max is the largest experimentally established external-load efficiency of isolated F1-ATPase hydrolysing ATP across its positive-power resisting-load range at the same temperature. Both measurements include consumed fuels, auxiliary chemical inputs and reset costs within the same energy boundary. Probe heat is excluded from load work. Chemical potentials, load, speed and uncertainties are specified.
completion.set_by: Atlas comparison criterion; no externally adopted completion threshold was found.
completion.basis: Searches covered MEXT Molecular Engine targets, CORDIS motor projects, molecular-ratchet reviews, and standards, prizes and efficiency targets; no external synthetic-motor completion threshold was found. This comparison defines biological efficiency using a chemical-to-mechanical motor. F1's reported near-100% stall efficiency is not a positive-power benchmark; its rotating-probe energy accounting also includes heat.

milestones.title: A synthetic motor maintains net directional motion while chemical fuel is supplied.
milestones.criterion: A synthetic motor has a nonzero net directional current while chemical fuel is supplied, without sequential changes of reaction conditions. Wilson and coauthors demonstrated this with a catenane, two interlocked molecular rings, using Fmoc-Cl fuel. Their bulk experiment used 2.6 μmol motor and inferred approximately one net 360° revolution per 12 h; the paper was published on 8 June 2016.
milestones.set_by: Community convention for chemical autonomy, stated by Wilson and coauthors and reviewed by Taticchi, Curcio and Corra.
milestones.threshold_quote: the components move directionally as long as a chemical fuel is present

milestones.title: A synthetic motor converts chemical fuel into positive mechanical work against a load.
milestones.criterion: Chemical fuel drives positive mechanical work against an opposing load, which may be elastic resistance. Wang and coauthors, published on 15 January 2025, demonstrated this in gel-1 specimens approximately 10×10×1 mm³. Contraction continued for seven days, with approximately 30% volume reduction inferred from projected area assuming isotropy. Reversing motor rotation powered expansion and renewed contraction.
milestones.set_by: Community convention for mechanical work, applied to synthetic catalysis-driven motors by Wang and coauthors in Nature.
milestones.threshold_quote: work against a load by a synthetic organocatalyst

milestones.title: A synthetic motor delivers positive steady-state mechanical power from chemical fuel.
milestones.criterion: In autonomous steady state, a synthetic motor has chemical input power P_chem>0 and external mechanical output power P_load>0, with no net depletion of stored free energy. For a contracting actuator, output is net work per contraction-and-reset cycle divided by cycle duration. The work-transducer convention gives η=P_load/P_chem>0. Wang's gel instead reaches a contraction plateau while fuel turnover continues.
milestones.set_by: Stochastic-thermodynamics convention for steady-state work transducers, summarized by Leighton and Sivak, section II.2.1, equation 6.
milestones.threshold_quote: For work transducers, thermodynamic efficiency can be defined in a straightforward manner as the ratio of output to input work,

results.finding: Gel-embedded synthetic motors showed directionally biased rotation; the gel sample contained approximately 0.08 mmol motor units.
results.detail: The directional bias was supported by a fuelled model compound and by gel contraction under a fixed fuelling system.
results.quote: Continuous 360° rotation of the rotor about the stator of the catalysis-driven motor-molecules incorporated in the polymeric framework of the gel twists the polymer chains of the cross-linked network around one another.

results.finding: A gel-1 specimen containing approximately 0.08 mmol motor units contracted by approximately 30% under chemical fuelling.
results.detail: Volume reduction was inferred from projected area assuming isotropy. Twisted polymer strands provided elastic resistance; reverse fuelling powered re-expansion and renewed contraction.
results.quote: The experimental demonstration of work against a load by a synthetic organocatalyst, and its mechanism of energy transduction

results.finding: A gel-1 specimen containing approximately 0.08 mmol motor units contracted for 7 days before reaching a plateau.
results.detail: Fuel turnover continued after contraction stopped. The reported contraction and separately fuelled reset do not establish positive net work per cycle or positive autonomous steady-state output power.
results.quote: Even after the gel stopped contracting, the catalysis of carbodiimide hydration by the gel-embedded motors continued as long as unreacted fuel remained or if the fuel was replenished.

results.finding: Synthetic dual motor 2a (5 μmol) sustained net directional contra-rotation at 0.24 rpm.
results.detail: Carbodiimide fuel was continuously supplied at a constant concentration for 100 minutes. Directionality was measured using a sterically blocked model motor, and rotation rates were inferred from fuel consumption.
results.quote:
Chemostating the fuel concentration
by syringe pump addition produced sustained repetitive contra-rotation
at a rate of 0.24 rpm for a period of 100 min.

results.finding: Synthetic phenylpyrrole motor, sample size not reported: approximately 24 forward rotations per backward rotation.
results.detail: Directionality was inferred from kinetic-gating measurements on a rotation-blocked motor model. Fuel was supplied continuously at low concentration.

results.finding: Azaindole-N-oxide molecular motor, sample size not reported: 0.24 net rotations per hour.
results.detail: Motor concentration was 0.83 mM. Directional rotation was quantified in situ during carbodiimide-fueled catalysis with a chiral hydrolysis promoter, without sequential changes of reaction conditions.
results.quote: Overall, this gives a rate of rotation of 0.24 rotations per hour

results.finding: BZ gel pump, sample size not reported: estimated generated power was 5.76 × 10−2 nW.
